summary: Simon Winant works in Indology and linguistics. Attested as a PhD student at Ghent University in 2026, he also served on the faculty there.
Siniruddha Dash works in Indology and linguistics. He served as Director at the University of Madras from 2000 to 2014 and became director at the K. V. Sarma Research Foundation in 2020.

Siran Upendra Deraniyagala (1942–2021) was an archaeologist who studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, the University of London under Frank Raymond Allchin, and Harvard. He was Director General of the Department of Archaeology from circa 1992 to 2001.

Sisir Roy works in philosophy and other fields, having studied under Debabrata SenSharma. He held posts as Professor at the Indian Statistical Institute and at the National Institute of Advanced Studies (attested 2009).
Siu-tong Kwan is a scholar of Buddhist studies and philosophy. He earned his PhD at the University of Hong Kong, where he was supervised by K. L. Dhammajoti, and also studied under Zhihua Yao.

Sivananda Saraswati (1887–1963) studied at Thanjavur Medical College around 1903–1905 before working in philosophy and religious studies. He taught Swami Vishnudevananda and founded the Divine Life Society in 1936 and the Yoga-Vedanta Forest Academy in 1948.
Smita Halder works in Indology and archaeology. Supervised by Susmita Basu Majumdar (attested 2026), she has been a Research Scholar/Fellow at the Asiatic Society (attested 2026).

So Takahashi is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology who completed an M.A. at the University of Tokyo. He held posts at Meijo University as Associate Professor (attested 1977–1978) and Professor (attested 1991).

Sodo Mori (b. 1934), a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology, studied at Komazawa and Tokyo universities under Kogen Mizuno, Hajime Nakamura, and G. P. Malalasekera. He held professorships at Josai and Aichi Gakuin universities.
Sodo Yokoyama (1907–1980) was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at Antai-ji from 1949 to 1957 under Kodo Sawaki, as well as under Eko Hashimoto.

Soen Nakagawa (1907–1984) was a Buddhist studies figure who studied at the First Higher School and the University of Tokyo, and under Gempo Yamamoto. His students included Robert Baker Aitken, Philip Kapleau, and John Daido Loori.

Sogen Omori (1904–1994) worked in Buddhist studies, philosophy, and religious studies, studying at Nihon University and under masters including Seisetsu Seki. He served as president of Hanazono University (1978–1982) and head priest of Koho-in.

Sogyal Rinpoche (1947–2019) was a Tibetan Buddhist teacher who studied at the universities of Delhi and Cambridge, as well as under Dudjom Rinpoche and Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche. He founded Rigpa in 1975.

Soiku Shigematsu (b. 1943) studied at Tokyo University of Foreign Studies, University of Tokyo, and Kyoto University. He was professor of English Literature at Shizuoka University (1975–2001) and professor at Kansai Medical University (2001–2006).

Sojo Hirano (1930–2011) was a Buddhist studies scholar who taught Sonja Arntzen and Yoel Hoffmann. He was an associate professor at Hanazono University (attested 1974) and shika at Zuigan-ji (attested 1992–1996).

Sokatsu Shaku (1870–1954) was a Zen figure who studied under Kosen Imakita and Soyen Shaku. He founded Tōkyō Ryōbōkai, Ryobokai Dojo of North America, and Ningen Zen, and taught Sokei-an Shigetsu Sasaki and Zuigan Goto.

Sokei-an Shigetsu Sasaki (1882–1945) was a Buddhist figure who studied at Tokyo Fine Arts School and under Sokatsu Shaku and Soyen Shaku. He founded the First Zen Institute of America and taught Alan Watts.

Sokichi Tsuda (1873–1961) was a scholar of history, archaeology, Sinology, and Japanology who studied at Tōkyō Senmon Gakkō. He held posts at the SMR Research Department, Waseda University, and the University of Tokyo.
Soko Morinaga (1925–1995) studied at Toyama High School, Daitoku-ji, and under Zuigan Goto and Sesso Oda. He served as head of Hanazono University (1986–1994) and abbot of Daishu-in.

Sokuo Eto (1888–1958) was a Buddhist studies scholar educated at Komazawa, Kyoto, and Tokyo universities. He served as president of Komazawa Junior College (circa 1950–1957) and as a professor at Komazawa University in 1953.
